title: Patron Saints of the UK
hook: Four nations, four saints: George, Andrew, David, Patrick — each with a feast day to remember.

facts.statement: The patron saint of England is **St George**, celebrated on **23rd April**.
The patron saint of Scotland is **St Andrew**, celebrated on **30th November**.
The patron saint of Wales is **St David**, celebrated on **1st March**.
The patron saint of Northern Ireland is **St Patrick**, celebrated on **17th March**.
St Patrick’s Day is an official **public holiday** in Northern Ireland.

title: Churches of the UK
hook: The monarch heads the Church of England; Wales and Northern Ireland have no established church at all.

facts.statement: **The monarch** is the head of the Church of England, and its spiritual leader is **the Archbishop of Canterbury**.
**St Augustine**, who led missionaries from Rome, became the first Archbishop of Canterbury.
The national Church of Scotland is a **Presbyterian** church.
There is **no established church** in Wales or Northern Ireland.

title: King James Bible & the Puritans
hook: King James I authorised an English Bible; the Puritans wanted worship stricter and plainer still.

facts.statement: King James I’s new English translation of the Bible is called the King James Version or the **Authorised Version**.
The Puritans were a group of **Protestants** who advocated strict and simple religious worship.

title: Christmas & Boxing Day
hook: The 25th celebrates the birth of Christ; the 26th, Boxing Day, keeps the holiday going.

facts.statement: **Christmas Day**, the **25th of December**, celebrates the birth of Jesus Christ.
Boxing Day, the day after Christmas Day, is a public holiday on **26th December**.

title: Easter, Lent & Good Friday
hook: Forty days of Lent lead to Good Friday and to Easter, always in March or April.

facts.statement: Easter takes place in **March or April**.
**The 40 days before Easter** are known as **Lent**.
**Good Friday** marks **the day when Jesus Christ died**.

title: Hogmanay & the New Year
hook: Scotland calls 31 December Hogmanay, and Auld Lang Syne sings in the New Year.

facts.statement: **Hogmanay** is **New Year’s Eve in Scotland**, the **31st of December**.
People in the UK and other countries sing **Auld Lang Syne** when celebrating the New Year.

title: Diwali & Eid al-Fitr
hook: Diwali is the Festival of Lights; Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan’s month of fasting.

facts.statement: Diwali, often called **the Festival of Lights**, is celebrated by **Hindus** and **Sikhs**.
**Eid al-Fitr** celebrates the end of Ramadan, when Muslims have fasted for a month.

title: Halloween & April Fool's Day
hook: Ghosts come out on 31 October; the newspapers print jokes until midday on 1 April.

facts.statement: **Halloween** is celebrated on the **31st of October**.
On **April Fool’s Day** the television and newspapers have stories that are jokes until midday.
**April Fool‘s Day**, 1 April, is the day when jokes are published in newspapers and telecast on TV.

title: Bank Holidays
hook: When the banks close and much of Britain closes with them, that is a bank holiday.

facts.statement: A bank holiday is **a public holiday when banks and many other businesses are closed for the day**.
Public holidays in the UK are known as **bank holidays**.

title: The Edinburgh Festival Fringe
hook: Every summer Edinburgh fills with festivals, and the Fringe is the biggest of them all.

facts.statement: The Edinburgh Festival Fringe (‘the Fringe’) takes place in **Edinburgh**, Scotland, every summer.

title: Flowers & Foods of the Nations
hook: Daffodil, thistle, shamrock — and haggis or an Ulster Fry to taste the nations.

facts.statement: The **daffodil** is the flower of Wales, **the thistle** of Scotland and **the shamrock** of Northern Ireland.
Haggis is a traditional food from **Scotland**; the traditional food of Northern Ireland is the **Ulster Fry**.

title: UK Currency: Coins & Banknotes
hook: Everything runs on pounds sterling — and Scottish and Northern Irish notes spend anywhere in the UK.

facts.statement: The currency in the UK is the **pound sterling** (symbol £).
UK currency has no **25p** coin and no **£25** banknote.
The highest-value standard UK banknote is **£50**, not £100.
facts.keyedNote: Some Scottish and Northern Irish banks do issue £100 notes; the test counts £50 as the highest standard note.

facts.statement: **Northern Ireland and Scotland** have their own banknotes, which are **valid everywhere in the UK**.

title: Working in the UK
hook: Prove your identity and your right to work, and the DWP issues your National Insurance number.

facts.statement: To get a National Insurance number you need **documents that prove your identity** and **documents that prove that you have permission to work in the UK**.
To arrange a National Insurance number, you **contact the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP)**.
**Women in Britain today make up about half of the workforce.**

title: School Governors
hook: Governors set a school's strategic direction and keep watch on its performance.

facts.statement: Key roles of school governors include **setting the strategic direction of the school** and **monitoring and evaluating school performance**.

title: Everyday Rules in the UK
hook: Licence at 17, moped at 16, alcohol at 18 — and every dog's collar names its owner.

facts.statement: When walking your dog in a public place, you must ensure **that your dog wears a collar showing the name and address of the owner**.
Out in public, a dog’s collar must show **the owner’s name** and **the owner’s address**.
You must be **18** to buy alcohol in the UK and **18** to go into betting shops or gambling clubs.
To drive on public roads you need **a valid driving licence** and must be at least **17 years old** for a car or motorcycle.
You must be at least **16 years old** to ride a moped in the UK.
Sunday and holiday hours are often shorter, but **most shops in the UK open seven days a week.**

title: UK Charities
hook: The National Trust minds Britain's places; Friends of the Earth minds the environment.

facts.statement: **The National Trust** is a charity that works to preserve important buildings, coastline and countryside in the UK.
**Friends of the Earth** is **an environmental charity**.

title: William Shakespeare
hook: England’s greatest playwright began life in the market town of Stratford-upon-Avon.

facts.statement: **William Shakespeare** was born in **Stratford-upon-Avon**, England.
Shakespeare’s most famous plays include **A Midsummer Night’s Dream** and **Macbeth**.

title: Wordsworth & The Daffodils
hook: A poet inspired by nature, Wordsworth made the daffodil the most famous flower in English poetry.

facts.statement: **William Wordsworth** wrote ‘The **Daffodils**’, his famous poem about that flower.
British poets such as **William Wordsworth** drew inspiration from nature.

title: Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales
hook: Pilgrims riding to Canterbury told stories on the way — Chaucer turned them into poems.

facts.statement: Geoffrey Chaucer’s **The Canterbury Tales** is a collection of **poems** about a group of people on a pilgrimage to Canterbury.

title: Great British fiction
hook: Sherlock Holmes, The Lord of the Rings and the Booker Prize — landmarks of British fiction.

facts.statement: **Sir Arthur Conan Doyle** wrote the Sherlock Holmes stories.
In 2003 **The Lord of the Rings** by JRR Tolkien was voted the country’s best-loved novel.
The Man Booker Prize is awarded annually for the best fiction novel, making it a prize for **literature**.

title: The Cenotaph, Whitehall
hook: The war memorial in Whitehall where the King and politicians gather for Remembrance Day.

facts.statement: The Cenotaph is **a war memorial** and the site of the annual Remembrance Day service.
The Cenotaph in Whitehall was designed by **Sir Edwin Lutyens**, who created many war memorials around the world.

title: Wren’s St Paul’s & Crathes Castle
hook: From the ashes of 1666 rose Wren’s St Paul’s; in Scotland stands Crathes Castle.

facts.statement: After the Great Fire of London in 1666, St Paul’s Cathedral was rebuilt to a design by the architect **Sir Christopher Wren**.
**Crathes Castle** is located in Scotland.

title: British stars of the screen
hook: From Chaplin’s silent tramp to Oscar nights, British actors made their mark in Hollywood.

facts.statement: **Charlie Chaplin** became famous in silent movies for playing **a tramp**.
British actresses Dame Judi Dench, Kate Winslet and Tilda Swinton have won Oscars, but **Emily Watson** has not.

title: British film successes
hook: Harry Potter, James Bond and Nick Park’s animations — British film is a global success story.

facts.statement: The two highest-grossing film franchises, **Harry Potter** and **James Bond**, were both produced in the UK.
Nick Park won three of his four Oscars for films featuring **Wallace and Gromit**, each one **an animated film**.
Academy Award winner Nick Park specialised in **animated movies**.

title: The BBC & broadcasting rules
hook: Funded by the licence fee, free of government control — and party coverage must be balanced by law.

facts.statement: The BBC is funded by the TV licence fee and is **independent of government**.
By law, radio and television coverage of political parties must be **balanced**, with **equal time** given to rival viewpoints.

title: British art & design
hook: Hockney’s pop art, Cliff’s Art Deco ceramics, the Tate in London and the Turner Prize.

facts.statement: **David Hockney** was an important contributor to the pop art movement of the 1960s.
**Clarice Cliff** was a famous designer of Art Deco ceramics.
The Turner Prize, established in 1984, is **a contemporary art award**, one of the most prestigious visual art awards in Europe.
The Tate Britain and Tate Modern galleries are in **London**.

title: Music & theatre in Britain
hook: Elgar at the Proms, the Beatles in the sixties and the West End’s Theatreland.

facts.statement: Sir Edward Elgar is remembered because **he was a musician**, best known for the Pomp and Circumstance Marches.
The Proms is **an eight-week summer season of daily orchestral classical music concerts**, held in venues including the Royal Albert Hall.
**The Beatles** and **The Rolling Stones** were two famous British pop groups of the Swinging Sixties.
London’s West End is known as **Theatreland** because of its many theatres.

title: British inventors & scientists
hook: Radar, the web, the Turing machine, split atoms and DNA — British minds led the way.

facts.statement: **William Caxton** was **the first person in England to print books using a printing press**.
Radar was developed by **Sir Robert Watson-Watt**.
In the 1930s the British mathematician Alan Turing invented **the Turing machine**, a theoretical mathematical device.
Scientists led by **Ernest Rutherford**, working at Manchester and then Cambridge, were the first to split the atom.
**Francis Crick** co-discovered **the structure of the DNA molecule** in the 1950s and was awarded a Nobel Prize for it.
The World Wide Web was invented by **Sir Tim Berners-Lee**.

title: Churchill & Florence Nightingale
hook: The public’s greatest Briton of all time, and the nurse who founded modern nursing.

facts.statement: In 2002 **Winston Churchill** was voted the greatest Briton of all time by the public.
Florence Nightingale was **a nurse** and is often regarded as the founder of modern nursing.

title: The UK & Great Britain
theme: Nations, capitals & geography of the UK
hook: Great Britain means England, Scotland and Wales; add Northern Ireland and you have the UK.

facts.statement: The UK is located in the **north west of Europe**.
Great Britain refers only to **England**, **Scotland** and **Wales** — Northern Ireland is **not** part of Great Britain.
The Union Flag, also known as the Union Jack, is **the Flag of the United Kingdom**.
The rose is the flower associated with **England**, as the thistle is with Scotland, the daffodil with Wales and the shamrock with Northern Ireland.

title: Crown Dependencies & Overseas Territories
theme: Nations, capitals & geography of the UK
hook: Channel Islands and Isle of Man sit near; St Helena and the Falklands lie far — none of them is part of the UK.

facts.statement: **The Channel Islands** and the **Isle of Man** are **Crown Dependencies** — self-governing islands closely linked to the UK but not part of it.
**St Helena** and **the Falkland Islands** are British overseas territories, linked to the UK but **not part** of the UK or Great Britain.

title: Capitals & Cities of the UK
theme: Nations, capitals & geography of the UK
hook: Beyond London: Edinburgh for Scotland, Cardiff for Wales, Belfast for Northern Ireland.

facts.statement: **Edinburgh** is the capital of Scotland, Cardiff is the capital of **Wales**, and **Belfast** is the capital of Northern Ireland.
Swansea, like Cardiff, is a city in **Wales**.

title: Landmarks of London
hook: Big Ben is the bell at Parliament, the Jewels sit in the Tower, and Whitehall keeps the Cenotaph.

facts.statement: Big Ben is the nickname for the great bell of the clock at **the Houses of the Parliament** in London.
The Crown Jewels are kept **at the Tower of London**.
Yeoman Warders, known as **Beefeaters**, give guided tours telling the history of **the Tower of London**.
**London’s West End**, also called ‘Theatreland’, is particularly well known for its theatres.
The **Cenotaph** is a war memorial located in Whitehall.

title: National Parks of Britain
hook: Britain has 15 national parks, and England’s largest is the Lake District.

facts.statement: National parks are **areas of protected countryside** that everyone can visit, and where people live, work and look after the landscape.
There are **15** national parks in England, Wales and Scotland.
**The Lake District**, in **England**, is the country’s **largest national park** and was voted Britain’s favourite view in 2007.
Snowdonia is a national park in **Wales**.
Loch Lomond and the Trossachs National Park is in the west of **Scotland**.

title: Famous Places Around the UK
hook: Stonehenge, the Giant’s Causeway, Skara Brae and the Eden Project — pin each one to its place on the map.

facts.statement: **Stonehenge** is a monument that stands in what is now the English county of Wiltshire.
The Giant’s Causeway, a formation of columns made from volcanic lava, is on the north-east coast of **Northern Ireland**.
Skara Brae, on Orkney off the north coast of **Scotland**, is the best preserved prehistoric village in northern Europe.
The Eden Project is located in **Cornwall**, in the south west of England.

title: Horse Racing in the UK
hook: The Grand National runs at Aintree, Royal Ascot in Berkshire, and the Scottish Grand National at Ayr.

facts.statement: The Grand National, run at Aintree near Liverpool, is a famous **horse racing** event.
**Royal Ascot** is a five-day horse-racing meeting in Berkshire attended by members of the Royal Family.
The Scottish Grand National takes place at **Ayr**.
The National Horseracing Museum is located in **Newmarket, Suffolk**.

title: Classic British Sporting Events
hook: Match each event to its sport: the Ashes is cricket, the Six Nations is rugby, Wimbledon is tennis.

facts.statement: The modern game of **golf** can be traced back to 15th century **Scotland**.
**The Ashes** is the most famous cricket competition, a series of Test matches played between England and Australia.
**The Six Nations Championship** is a rugby union competition between England, Ireland, Scotland, Wales, France and Italy.
**Wimbledon**, played each year at the All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club, is the most famous tennis tournament in the UK.
**The University of Oxford** and **the University of Cambridge** compete in a popular yearly rowing race on the River Thames.

title: Olympic & Paralympic Britain
hook: The Games came to Britain in 1908, 1948 and 2012 — remember the Paralympic champions too.

facts.statement: The UK has hosted **the Olympic games** on **3** occasions: 1908, 1948 and 2012.
Mary Peters, who moved to Northern Ireland as a child, won an Olympic **gold** medal in the pentathlon in 1972.
**Baroness Tanni Grey-Thompson** and **Ellie Simmonds** are two of Britain’s most famous Paralympians.
**Ellie Simmonds** won gold medals for swimming at the 2008, 2012 and 2016 Paralympic Games.

title: British Sporting Heroes
hook: 1954: Bannister breaks the four-minute mile; 1966: Bobby Moore lifts the World Cup.

facts.statement: **Bobby Moore** captained the English football team that won the World Cup in 1966.
In 1954 **Sir Roger Bannister** made sporting history: **he was the first man in the world to run a mile in under four minutes.**

title: The UK’s Diverse Population
hook: About one person in ten in the UK has a parent or grandparent born outside the country.

facts.statement: **Around 10%** of the UK population has a parent or grandparent born outside the UK.

title: Responsibilities of UK citizens
hook: Five duties, one theme: look after yourself, your family, your area, the law and other people's rights.

facts.statement: Your duties include: **to respect and obey the law**, **to look after yourself and your family** and **to look after the area in which you live and the environment**.
You should also aim **to look after yourself and your family** and **to respect the rights of others, including their right to their own opinions**.
The National Citizen Service programme is **optional** and gives **16- and 17-year-olds** the chance to develop their skills and take part in a community project.

title: Fundamental principles of British life
hook: Democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, tolerance, participation – five pillars worth reciting.

facts.statement: The fundamental principles of British life include **democracy**, **the rule of law** and **individual liberty**, along with tolerance of different faiths and beliefs.

title: Parliament: Commons & Lords
hook: Commons elected, Lords appointed – remember which house is which and who sits in each.

facts.statement: The UK Parliament is formed of two chambers: the **House of Commons** and **the House of Lords**.
Several Church of England **bishops sit in the House of Lords**.
Peers gain their seats in the House of Lords by **appointment rather than election**, with life peers appointed by **the monarch** on the Prime Minister's advice.
Prime Minister's Questions takes place **every week** while Parliament is sitting.
Proceedings in Parliament are broadcast on television and published in official reports called **Hansard**.

title: MPs & the Speaker
hook: MPs serve a place: everyone in the constituency, reachable by letter, phone or a local surgery.

facts.statement: MPs **represent everyone in their constituency** and **help to create new laws**, as well as scrutinising the government and debating national issues.
You can contact MPs **by letter or telephone**, at their **constituency office** or their office in the House of Commons, and many hold local surgeries.
Debates in the House of Commons are chaired by **the Speaker**, who is also **an MP** representing a constituency and its constituents.

title: Ministers, civil servants & opposition
hook: Home Secretary, home front: crime, policing and immigration all land on one desk.

facts.statement: **The Home Secretary** is the minister responsible for **crime**, **policing** and immigration.
Civil servants are not political appointees – **they are chosen on merit and are politically neutral**.
Senior opposition MPs, appointed by the leader of the opposition, form the **Shadow Cabinet** to challenge the government and offer alternative policies.
The official home of the Prime Minister is **10 Downing Street**.

title: The UK constitution
hook: There is no single document to read – the British constitution is famously unwritten.

facts.statement: The British constitution is **not written down in any single document**, which is why it is described as 'unwritten'.
The system of government in the UK is a **parliamentary democracy**.
Constitutional institutions include the monarchy, Parliament, the cabinet, the judiciary, the police and the civil service – but not **the armed forces**.
Towns, cities and rural areas in the UK are governed by **democratically elected councils**, often called 'local authorities'.

title: General elections & voting
hook: Every 5 years a poll card arrives; when an MP quits mid-term, a by-election follows.

facts.statement: MPs are elected at a general election, which is held at least **every 5 years**.
The voting age for UK general elections was set at **18** in 1969.
Before a general election takes place, you will be sent **a poll card**.
If an MP dies or resigns, a fresh election called a **by-election** is held in his or her constituency.
By law, **television** and **radio** coverage of political parties must be balanced, with equal time given to rival viewpoints.
**Persuading people to vote for a political party**, by knocking on doors or handing out leaflets, is called 'canvassing'.

title: Registering & standing for election
hook: Eighteen opens the door to standing for office; Northern Ireland registers each voter individually.

facts.statement: **Northern Ireland** uses a system called '**individual registration**', where all those entitled to vote must complete their own registration form.
Most citizens of the UK, the Irish Republic or the Commonwealth aged **18** or over can stand for public office, including election as an MP.

title: Margaret Thatcher
hook: The Iron Lady claimed two records: first woman PM and longest-serving PM of the 20th century.

facts.statement: **Margaret Thatcher** made history because **she was the first woman Prime Minister of the UK**.
**Margaret Thatcher** was the longest-serving Prime Minister of the 20th century, in office from 1979 until 1990.

title: Prime Ministers through history
hook: From Walpole in 1721 to the 2010 coalition, the same office keeps changing hands.

facts.statement: The first man to be called Prime Minister was **Sir Robert Walpole**, who held office from 1721 to 1742.
**Winston Churchill** became Prime Minister and was an inspirational leader to the British people during the Second World War.
In 1945 the British people elected a Labour government, and the new Prime Minister was **Clement Attlee**.
**John Major** became Prime Minister after Margaret Thatcher and played an important part in the Northern Ireland peace process.
The Labour government led by **Tony Blair**, elected in 1997, introduced a Scottish Parliament and a Welsh Assembly.
In May 2010 **the Conservative Party** and **the Liberal Democrats Party** formed a coalition, with David Cameron becoming Prime Minister.

title: The role of the monarch
hook: The monarch appoints the government but does not run it: advise, warn, encourage.

facts.statement: The monarch has two duties: **to appoint the government**, and **to advise, warn and encourage the Prime Minister‘s decisions on government policies**.
facts.keyedNote: More precisely, the monarch advises, warns and encourages the Prime Minister; the decisions themselves are made by the PM and cabinet.

title: What the devolved nations control
hook: Devolved bodies run health and schools; defence and immigration never left London.

facts.statement: The devolved administrations control many public services and can pass laws on **health** and **education**.
**Defence** and **immigration** policy remain under central UK government control – the Northern Ireland Assembly and other devolved bodies cannot decide them.
The Scottish Parliament can legislate on civil and criminal law, health, **education**, planning and additional tax-raising powers.

title: The Senedd & NI Assembly
hook: Remember 60 and 90: Senedd members and Northern Ireland MLAs, both elected proportionally.

facts.statement: The Welsh Parliament (Senedd) has **60** members, elected **every 4 years** by a form of proportional representation.
The Northern Ireland Assembly has **90** elected members, known as MLAs, chosen **by a system of proportional representation**.
The Northern Ireland Assembly has been **suspended on a few occasions** by the UK government.

title: Juries in the UK
hook: One register, two duties: it lets you vote and can call you, at random, to a jury at 18.

facts.statement: Jurors are selected **randomly from the electoral register**, so that is where you must be registered to be called.
Anyone on the electoral register aged **18** to 70 can be asked to serve on a jury.
A jury has **12** members in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, but **15** members in Scotland.

title: Criminal courts & Youth Courts
hook: Minor crime goes to magistrates – and in Youth Courts, young names stay out of the papers.

facts.statement: In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, most minor criminal cases are dealt with in a **Magistrates’ Court**.
In Scotland, minor criminal offences go to **the Justice of the Peace Court**.
In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, Youth Court cases are normally heard by **up to 3 specially trained magistrates** or **a District Judge**.
Cases in a Youth Court are heard by **district judges** or **specially trained magistrates**.
The name or photographs of a young person accused in a Youth Court **cannot be published in newspapers or used by the media**.

title: Criminal vs civil law
hook: If it harms the public it is criminal; workplace and money disputes stay civil.

facts.statement: Racial crime and **smoking in public places where it is not allowed** are examples of **criminal offences**.
**Discrimination in the workplace** is an example of civil law rather than criminal law.

title: Solicitors & small claims
hook: Time is money at a solicitor's office; small claims let you skip the lawyer entirely.

facts.statement: **Solicitors’ charges are usually based on how much time they spend on a case**.
The small claims procedure is **an informal way of helping people to settle minor disputes without spending a lot of time and money using a lawyer**.
Small claims are used for amounts under £10,000 in England and Wales, and under **£5,000** in Scotland and Northern Ireland.

title: Dealing with the police
hook: A police complaint has many doors: the station, the Chief Constable or an independent body.

facts.statement: Anyone can complain about the police – **go to the police station directly** or **write to the Chief Constable of the police force involved**.
Writing to the Chief Constable is only one route – police complaints can also go to **independent bodies** such as the Independent Police Complaints Commission.
If you think someone is trying to persuade you to join an extremist or terrorist cause, notify **your local police force**.

title: Laws that protect people
hook: The law reaches inside the home: partner violence, forced marriage and FGM are all crimes.

facts.statement: If a husband forces his wife to have sex, he **can be charged with rape**.
Anyone who is violent towards their partner – whether man or woman, married or living together – **can be prosecuted**.
Female genital mutilation (FGM), or taking a girl or woman abroad for FGM, is **illegal in the UK and a criminal offence**.
Court orders **can be obtained to protect a person from being forced into a marriage**.

title: Early Britain: Stone to Iron Age
hook: Hunter-gatherers came first, farmers followed 6,000 years ago, and Iron Age kings put their names on the first coins.

facts.statement: The first people to live in Britain, in the Stone Age, were **hunter-gatherers**.
The first farmers arrived in Britain **6,000 years ago**, and their ancestors probably came from **south-east Europe**.
**The people of the Iron Age** made the first coins to be minted in Britain, some inscribed with **the names of Iron Age kings**.

title: Roman Britain
hook: Caesar tried first in 55 BC, Boudicca fought back, and Hadrian built a wall to keep out the Picts.

facts.statement: **Julius Caesar** led the first Roman invasion of Britain, in 55 BC.
**Boudicca**, queen of the Iceni in eastern England, was a tribal leader who fought against **the Romans**.
**Emperor Hadrian** built a wall in the north of England to keep out the Picts, ancestors of the Scottish people.
Hadrian’s Wall included the forts of **Housesteads** and **Vindolanda**.

title: Anglo-Saxons and the Vikings
hook: After Rome left in AD 410 the Jutes, Angles and Saxons arrived; Alfred the Great later united England against the Vikings.

facts.statement: After the Romans left in AD 410, Britain was invaded by tribes from northern Europe: **the Jutes**, the Angles and the Saxons.
The Anglo-Saxon kingdoms in England united under **King Alfred the Great**, who defeated the Vikings.

title: William the Conqueror & 1066
hook: One 1066 conquest left England a tapestry, a great survey and a tower — all pointing back to William.

facts.statement: **The Norman Conquest** of **1066** was the last successful foreign invasion of England.
William the Conqueror was the Duke of Normandy, in what is now northern **France**, and defeated Harold, the Saxon king, at Hastings in 1066.
**The Battle of Hastings**, William’s victory of 1066, is commemorated in a great embroidery known as the Bayeux Tapestry.
Two records that give us information about England under William I are **the Domesday Book** and **the Bayeux Tapestry**.
**William the Conqueror** introduced **the Domesday Book**, drawn up **after the Norman conquest** to list England’s towns, people, land and animals.
**William the Conqueror** built the Tower of London, whose Norman castle keep is **the White Tower**.

title: Magna Carta, 1215
hook: 1215 is the year the law was set above the king.

facts.statement: The Magna Carta, created in **1215**, established that even the king was subject to the law — **it restricted the King’s power**.

title: Battle of Bannockburn, 1314
hook: 1314 at Bannockburn: Robert the Bruce’s Scots beat the English, and Scotland stayed unconquered.

facts.statement: In 1314 the Scottish, led by **Robert the Bruce**, defeated the English at the Battle of Bannockburn, and Scotland remained unconquered by the English.

title: The Black Death, 1348
hook: One arrival in 1348 — the plague called the Black Death — killed a third of England.

facts.statement: In 1348, during **the Middle Ages**, a disease known as **the Black Death**, probably **a plague**, came to Britain.
The Black Death killed **one third of the population** of England, with a similar proportion in Scotland and Wales.

title: Medieval England: War, Land, Language
hook: A 116-year war with France, serfs on a lord’s land, and two languages merging into English.

facts.statement: In the Middle Ages, English kings fought a long war with France called **the Hundred Years War**, which actually lasted 116 years.
Medieval serfs were **peasants who had a small area of their lord’s agricultural land**, where they could grow food.
After the Norman Conquest, nobles spoke **Norman French** and peasants spoke **Anglo-Saxon**; these two languages combined into one English language.
**William Caxton** was the first person in England to print books using a printing press.

title: The Wars of the Roses
hook: Two families, two roses: York against Lancaster.

facts.statement: The Wars of the Roses were fought between the supporters of two families: **the House of York** and **the House of Lancaster**.

title: Henry VIII & the Reformation
hook: A refused divorce led Henry VIII to break with the Pope and found the Church of England.

facts.statement: **Henry VIII** established the Church of England **because the Pope didn’t let him divorce his first wife, Catherine of Aragon**.
**The Reformation** was the movement against the authority of the Pope and the ideas of the Catholic Church during the reign of Henry VIII.
Anne Boleyn, the wife of Henry VIII, was executed at the **Tower of London**.
**Henry VIII** was the father of Queen Elizabeth I.

title: Mary, Queen of Scots
hook: Scotland turned Protestant in 1560, but its queen Mary Stuart stayed Catholic and was finally executed.

facts.statement: In 1560 the Scottish Parliament abolished the Pope’s authority and Scotland established **a Protestant church** with an elected leadership.
**Mary Stuart (‘Mary, Queen of Scots’) was a Catholic**.
After 20 years in prison, Mary, Queen of Scots, was accused of plotting against Elizabeth I and **she was executed.**

title: Elizabeth I & the Spanish Armada
hook: 1588 is the year Protestant England, under Elizabeth I, defeated the Armada Spain sent to restore Catholicism.

facts.statement: In **1588** the English defeated **the Spanish Armada**, a large fleet of ships sent by **Spain** to conquer England and restore Catholicism.
**Elizabeth I was a Protestant and she succeeded in finding a balance between the views of the Catholics and the more extreme Protestants.**
Elizabeth I was not a Catholic; **she was a Protestant**.

title: The Early Stuarts & the Civil War
hook: Divine right met Parliament's army — the king lost his head and England, briefly, its monarchy.

facts.statement: When Elizabeth I died, her cousin King James VI of **Scotland** also became King James I of England, Wales and Ireland.
Charles I believed in the ‘Divine Right of Kings’ and tried **to rule without the Parliament**.
In the Civil War from 1642, **the Cavaliers and the Roundheads** fought — the Cavaliers for King Charles I, the Roundheads for Parliament.
In the Civil War, Charles I's army was defeated at **the Battle of Marston Moor** and **the Battle of Naseby**.
**Charles I** was held prisoner by the parliamentary army, and in 1649 **he was executed**.
**When Charles I was executed**, England declared itself a republic, called the Commonwealth, with no monarch.

title: Cromwell & the escape of Charles II
hook: The man who ruled Britain without a crown — and the king who survived by hiding in an oak tree.

facts.statement: **Oliver Cromwell** was given the title of Lord Protector and ruled until his death in 1658.
Defeated by Cromwell in the Civil War, **Charles II** famously escaped by **hiding in an oak tree** before fleeing to Europe.

title: Charles II & the Restoration
hook: Charles II came back from the Netherlands to a reign of fire, refugees and new rights for prisoners.

facts.statement: In May 1660 Parliament invited **Charles II** to come back from exile in the Netherlands, and he was crowned king.
During Charles II's reign **a fire** destroyed much of London, including many churches and St Paul's Cathedral.
The Habeas Corpus Act became law in 1679 and guaranteed **that every prisoner has a right to a court hearing**.
Between 1680 and 1720 many refugees called Huguenots came to England from **France**.

title: The Glorious Revolution, 1688
hook: A king replaced without resistance, and a Bill that set the limits of royal power — 1688 changed the rules.

facts.statement: In 1688 important Protestants asked **William of Orange** to invade England, and his unresisted takeover was called **the ‘Glorious Revolution’**.
William of Orange defeated **James II** at the Battle of the Boyne in Ireland in 1690.
The laws passed after the Glorious Revolution marked the beginning of the **constitutional monarchy**.
The Bill of Rights, 1689, confirmed **the rights of Parliament and the limits of the king's power**, not a right to vote for men or women.
**The MacDonalds of Glencoe** were the Scottish clan killed for not taking the oath.

title: Bonnie Prince Charlie & the Highlands
hook: The last Stuart bid for the throne rose with the Highland clans; later the crofts were cleared for sheep.

facts.statement: In 1745 Charles Edward Stuart — **Bonnie Prince Charlie** — raised an army supported by clansmen from **the Highlands** of Scotland.
In **the Highland Clearances**, many Scottish landlords destroyed small farms known as ‘crofts’ to make space for flocks of sheep and cattle.

title: The Enlightenment
hook: The 18th century rethought politics, philosophy and science — Smith on economics, Hume on human nature.

facts.statement: **The Enlightenment**, during the 18th century, was **a period when new ideas about politics, philosophy and science were developed**.
During the Enlightenment, Adam Smith developed ideas about **economics** which are still referred to today.
During the Enlightenment, David Hume developed ideas about human nature that continue to influence **philosophy**.

title: Isaac Newton & gravity
hook: One book, the Principia, showed how gravity applied to the whole universe.

facts.statement: Isaac Newton is famous for **the discovery of gravity**: his Principia Mathematica showed how gravity applied to the whole universe.

title: The Industrial Revolution
hook: Steam power made Britain the first country to industrialise — bringing canals, railways and new factory laws.

facts.statement: **The steam power** behind new machinery drove the Industrial Revolution — Britain's rapid industrial development of the 18th and 19th centuries.
During the 18th century, **manufacturing** jobs became the biggest source of employment in Britain.
Canals were built **to link the factories to towns and cities and to the ports**, particularly in the middle and north of England.
The Factories Act of 1847 was important because **it limited the number of hours that women and children could work to 10 hours per day**.
The engineer Isambard Kingdom Brunel, builder of tunnels, bridges and ships, was responsible for **the construction of the Great Western Railway**.

title: 20th-century British inventions
hook: Jet engines, television and Concorde — British invention did not stop with steam.

facts.statement: The **jet engine** was developed in Britain in the 1930s by Sir Frank Whittle.
The **television** was developed by the Scotsman John Logie Baird in the 1920s.
**Britain** and **France** together developed Concorde, the world's only supersonic commercial airliner.

title: Victorian free trade & the Great Exhibition
hook: Import taxes fell and the Crystal Palace rose — free-trade Britain put itself on display in 1851.

facts.statement: Victorian governments promoted free trade by **abolishing a number of taxes on imported goods**, such as repealing the Corn Laws in 1846.
The Great Exhibition of 1851 opened in Hyde Park in **the Crystal Palace**, a huge building made of steel and glass.

title: Ireland in the 19th century
hook: A failed potato crop cost a million lives, while Fenians pressed for complete independence from the UK.

facts.statement: In the middle of the 19th century the **potato** crop failed and Ireland suffered a famine in which a million people died.
The Irish Nationalist movement grew through the 19th century, and some, called the **Fenians**, favoured complete independence.

title: American colonies win independence
hook: Tax colonists who have no say in Parliament and you may lose them — in 1776, thirteen colonies left.

facts.statement: The American colonies came to want independence because **the British government wanted to tax them**.
In 1776, 13 **North American** colonies declared their independence, demanding ‘no taxation without representation’.

title: Trafalgar & Waterloo
hook: Nelson fell winning at Trafalgar; Wellington finished Napoleon at Waterloo, the last battle between Britain and France.

facts.statement: **Admiral Nelson** was in charge of the British fleet at **the Battle of Trafalgar** and was killed in the battle.
In 1815 the Duke of Wellington defeated the French Emperor Napoleon at **the Battle of Waterloo** — the last battle between Britain and **France**.

title: Abolition of slavery
hook: A politician's long campaign paid off in 1833, when the Emancipation Act freed the Empire's slaves.

facts.statement: In **1833** the Emancipation Act **abolished slavery throughout the British Empire**.
William Wilberforce was **a politician** — a member of Parliament — who helped turn public opinion against the slave trade.

title: Exploration & the growing empire
hook: Elizabethan settlers in America, Cook charting Australia — an empire built on trade, and contested with France.

facts.statement: In **Elizabeth I**'s time, English settlers first began to colonise the eastern coast of America.
Captain **James Cook** mapped the coast of Australia, and a few colonies were established there.
In the 18th century Britain's trading and settlements overseas brought conflict with **France**, which was expanding in the same areas of the world.

title: The Crimean War
hook: Britain, Turkey and France against Russia — the first war the public followed in news stories and photographs.

facts.statement: From 1853 to 1856 Britain fought with Turkey and France against **Russia** in the Crimean War.
**The Crimean War** was the first war to be extensively covered by the media, through news stories and photographs.

title: The Boer War, 1899-1902
hook: Settlers from the Netherlands — the Boers — held off the British Empire in South Africa for over three years.

facts.statement: **The Boer War** of 1899 to 1902 took place in **South Africa**, then part of the British Empire.
In South Africa the British fought settlers from the Netherlands called the **Boers**, who fought fiercely for over three years.

title: The Suffragettes & Votes for Women
hook: Pankhurst's suffragettes won the vote in steps — over-30s in 1918, equal at 21 in 1928 — with war work tipping the scales.

facts.statement: **Emmeline Pankhurst** was **a suffragette** — the leader of the suffragettes — and fought for **the right for women to vote**.
Campaigners for women's right to vote formed the women's suffrage movement and became known as the **suffragettes**.
In **1918** women over 30 were given the vote, partly **in recognition of the contribution women made to the war effort during the First World War**.
In **1928**, **women were given the right to vote at the age of 21, the same as men.**

title: The First World War
hook: The assassination of Austria's Archduke in 1914 started it; the guns stopped at 11.00 am on 11th November 1918.

facts.statement: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria in 1914 set off a chain of events leading to **the First World War**.
The First World War came to an end **in 1918** — **at 11.00 am on 11th November 1918** — with victory for Britain and its allies.

title: The Second World War
hook: Germany invaded Poland in 1939; the RAF fought the Battle of Britain and small boats helped rescue over 300,000 men at Dunkirk.

facts.statement: The Second World War began when Hitler's Germany invaded **Poland** in **1939**, and Britain and France declared war to stop his aggression.
**The Battle of Britain**, fought in the summer of 1940 by **the Royal Air Force**, was **an aerial battle** between Britain and Germany.
The 'Dunkirk spirit' recalls **the evacuation of Allied soldiers from France during World War II**, when small boats helped the Navy rescue over 300,000 men.

title: Ireland: Home Rule to Republic
hook: Home Rule was promised in 1913, put on hold by world war — and in 1949 Ireland became a republic.

facts.statement: Home Rule, promised for Ireland in 1913, was delayed until 1921 **due to the outbreak of the First World War**.
Ireland became a republic in **1949**.

title: Admiral Nelson & Trafalgar
hook: Nelson commanded the British fleet at Trafalgar against the combined French and Spanish fleet and was killed in the battle.

facts.statement: **Admiral Nelson** was **a British officer in charge of the British fleet at the Battle of Trafalgar against the Spanish fleet** allied with the French.
facts.keyedNote: The keyed option names only the Spanish fleet; Nelson in fact fought the combined French and Spanish fleet at Trafalgar.

title: The Great Depression in Britain
hook: In the 1930s slump Britain's traditional heavy industries — shipbuilding above all — were hit hardest.

facts.statement: During the Great Depression of the 1930s, traditional heavy industries such as **shipbuilding** were badly affected.

title: Post-war Britain
hook: Free secondary schools, a new United Nations, the Swinging Sixties and Concorde — how Britain changed from 1944 on.

facts.statement: The United Nations, which aims to prevent war and promote international peace and security, was set up **after the Second World War.**
The Education Act 1944, often called 'the Butler Act', introduced **free secondary education in England and Wales**.
The **1960s**, the 'Swinging Sixties', saw **a growth in British fashion and pop music**, the rise of The Beatles, and liberalised social laws.
Britain and **France** together developed Concorde, the world's only supersonic commercial airliner.

title: The Commonwealth
hook: Most Commonwealth members were once part of the British Empire; they work together on democracy and development.

facts.statement: The Commonwealth is **an association of countries that support each other and work together towards shared goals in democracy and development.**
